message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"19.16","text":"Simon said in reply, “Concerning the evil one, what else have I left to say except that God made him from non-existent things, and in this respect the maker is evil: he made what did not exist come to be, even though he was able to make him good, since the one who came into being possessed no nature of his own with respect to choosing evil.” Peter said, “Making him from non-existent things with choice is similar to the argument we stated before: that by making his temperament such that he delights in evils, God himself appears responsible for what came into being. Since, then, there is one resolution for both questions, we will say later why he made him delight in the destruction of evil people.” Simon said, “If he made the angels too with power over themselves, but the evil one departed from being righteous, why has he been honored with rulership? The one who honored him appears, through the very thing with which he honored him, to delight in evils.” Peter said, “If, after he departed, God appointed him to rule over those like him and commanded him to inflict punishment on sinners according to law, God is not unjust. But if the objection is that he honored him after he departed, the one who honored him foresaw the benefit: both that the honor is temporary and that it is right for evil people to be ruled by an evil one and, when they sin, to be punished by him.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"Περὶ πονηροῦ","chosen":"Concerning the evil one","rationale":"The masculine adjective is substantival and is subsequently treated as a personal agent; “concerning evil” would obscure that personification."},{"source_quote":"ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων","chosen":"from non-existent things","rationale":"This preserves the plural philosophical expression rather than replacing it with the familiar but less source-transparent “from nothing.”"},{"source_quote":"προαίρεσιν ἔχοντα","chosen":"with choice","rationale":"The phrase describes the created being as possessing deliberate choice; “free will” would add a more systematized technical formulation."},{"source_quote":"τὴν κρᾶσιν","chosen":"his temperament","rationale":"Here κρᾶσις denotes the being’s constitution or temperamental mixture, not merely an act of mixing."},{"source_quote":"ἀρχῇ τετίμηται","chosen":"has been honored with rulership","rationale":"ἀρχή here denotes governing authority rather than simply a beginning or abstract honor."},{"source_quote":"τοὺς κακοὺς ὑπὸ κακοῦ ἄρχεσθαι","chosen":"for evil people to be ruled by an evil one","rationale":"The rendering preserves the repetition of κακός for the ruled people and their evil ruler."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"19.17","text":"Simon said, “Can it be that, because he has always existed, he thus abolishes sole rule, since another power—the power associated with matter—rules jointly?” Peter said, “If they differ in their essences, they also differ in their powers, and the stronger rules the weaker. But if they are of the same essence, then they prove to be equal in power and alike good or evil. Yet it is evident that they are not equal in power, for matter was brought by the creator into whatever form of a world he wished. Indeed, it cannot be said that it always existed as an essence rather than as matter, as God’s storehouse. For it cannot be said, ‘There was ..... when God was without possessions’; rather, he alone was always its ruler. Therefore also eternal μο ........; and on this hypothesis one might rightly speak of both the ruler and the ........́.ου. as existing.” Simon said, “What, then? Did the evil one make himself? And is God good in this way—that, although he knew the evil one would be bent on evil, he did not destroy him as he was coming into being, when, being incomplete, he was capable of being destroyed? For if he came into being suddenly, and perfect at that, he consequently wages war against the creator as one who suddenly became equal to him in power.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὰ τῆς μοναρχίας","chosen":"sole rule","rationale":"μοναρχία concerns rule by one; “monarchy” is possible but could suggest a merely political institution in modern English."},{"source_quote":"τῆς κατὰ τὴν ὕλην δυνάμεως","chosen":"the power associated with matter","rationale":"κατά with the accusative characterizes the power in relation to matter without deciding whether it belongs to, inheres in, or operates through matter."},{"source_quote":"ταῖς οὐσίαις","chosen":"in their essences","rationale":"The argument concerns ontological substance or essence, not merely material possessions."},{"source_quote":"ἡ ὕλη εἰς οἷον ἠθέλησε κόσμου ἠνέχθη σχῆμα","chosen":"matter was brought by the creator into whatever form of a world he wished","rationale":"The passive ἠνέχθη presents matter as subjected to the creator’s chosen cosmic form."},{"source_quote":"ὡς θεοῦ ταμεῖον","chosen":"as God’s storehouse","rationale":"ταμεῖον can denote a storehouse, treasury, or inner chamber; “storehouse” suits the portrayal of matter as material held at God’s disposal."},{"source_quote":"καὶ ταῦτα τέλειος","chosen":"and perfect at that","rationale":"καὶ ταῦτα adds emphatic force: the sudden appearance is posited as occurring in a fully developed state."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"Ἦν ..... ὅτε","issue":"The selected edition contains a confirmed five-dot printed lacuna between Ἦν and ὅτε. Its content is unavailable; the translation retains all five dots and supplies no restoration.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"διὸ καὶ ἀίδιος μο ........ καὶ","issue":"A confirmed eight-dot printed lacuna follows the surviving fragment μο and interrupts the clause. The fragment and all eight dots are retained, without assigning an otherwise unattested completion.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"τοῦ ........́.ου.","issue":"The final coordinated genitive contains a confirmed lacunose word with surviving ending ου and printed dots. The incomplete form is preserved in the translation because no full lexical rendering can be established from the selected edition alone.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"19.18","text":"Peter said, “You are saying impossibilities. For even while he was coming into being little by little, God was able, by his own choice, to destroy him as an enemy. And foreknowing that he would not become good, he would not have permitted him to come into being unless he knew that his coming into being would be useful to him. Nor could he have become perfect suddenly from himself, for one who did not yet exist could not fashion himself; nor can anything that possesses essence come into being from non-existent things. And since he is generated, no one could rightly say that he is eternally equal in power.” Simon said, “Then is it one of the relative things, and is it evil in this way—evil as water is to fire, but good to earth that thirsts out of season? In the same way, iron is good for farming but evil for murders; desire is not evil for marriages but is grievous for adultery; killing is evil, but to the killer it is good in relation to what he has planned; greed is evil, but pleasant to the greedy person; and everything else of this kind follows the same pattern. Yet according to this argument neither is evil evil nor does good prove to be good, for each produces the other. Does not, indeed, what seems to be done badly delight the doer but punish the sufferer? And if it seems unjust that one who has loved himself should delight himself as much as possible and for that reason suffer harsh treatment from a righteous judge for having loved himself, to whom does it not seem unjust?”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ προαιρέσει ἀνελεῖν ἠδύνατο","chosen":"God was able, by his own choice, to destroy him","rationale":"The main rendering treats God as the continuing subject and preserves both agency and deliberate choice. The phrase’s attachment is compressed and could alternatively be understood as emphasizing that the evil one was destroyed “by him” because of a choice."},{"source_quote":"οὔτε ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων γενέσθαι τί οὐσίαν ἔχει δύναται","chosen":"nor can anything that possesses essence come into being from non-existent things","rationale":"τί is taken indefinitely as “anything,” while οὐσία denotes actual essence or substance."},{"source_quote":"τῶν· πρὸς τί","chosen":"one of the relative things","rationale":"τὰ πρός τι is the philosophical category of things defined in relation to something else; the edition’s intervening punctuation does not change that contextual sense."},{"source_quote":"τῇ ἀκαίρως διψώσῃ γῇ","chosen":"to earth that thirsts out of season","rationale":"ἀκαίρως literally marks the earth’s thirst as untimely or unseasonable; it has not been softened to the generic “dry earth.”"},{"source_quote":"ἑκάτερον γὰρ τὸ ἕτερον ἐργάζεται","chosen":"for each produces the other","rationale":"The clause claims reciprocal production or effect between the two categories rather than merely saying that each can be renamed."},{"source_quote":"χαλεπὰ πείσεσθαι","chosen":"suffer harsh treatment","rationale":"The idiom means to undergo grievous or harsh things, here imposed by a judge."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ προαιρέσει","issue":"The agency phrase ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ and the dative προαιρέσει have uncertain attachment within an active infinitival construction. The translation takes both as emphasizing God’s agency and deliberate choice; an alternative is to connect the choice with the evil one’s status as an enemy.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"τῶν· πρὸς τί","issue":"The printed stop divides the standard philosophical expression τῶν πρὸς τί. Context supports reading the words together as “the relative things”; this is treated as editorial punctuation, not as an OCR defect.","proposed_reading":"τῶν πρὸς τί","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"τὸ ἑαυτὸν ἀγαπήσαντα. εὐφραίνειν","issue":"The printed period separates the articular accusative participle from the infinitive needed to continue its construction. The translation reads the syntax continuously while retaining the wording of the selected edition.","proposed_reading":"τὸ ἑαυτὸν ἀγαπήσαντα εὐφραίνειν","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"19.19","text":"Peter said, “One must then punish oneself through self-control whenever desire wishes to rush toward harming another, knowing that the evil one can kill evil people, since from the beginning he has received authority against them. This is therefore evil for those who have done evil; but for their souls to remain under punishment after their killing—this truly is grievous, when someone rightly says that the one foreassigned to evil is rightly placed. For this reason one must avoid, as I said, wronging another for the sake of brief pleasure, so that one does not cast oneself into everlasting punishment for the sake of a little pleasure.” Simon said, “Then is there nothing evil or good by nature, but does it differ by law and custom ..̓̀. among the Persians it is their own practice to marry mothers, sisters, and daughters, whereas among others it is forbidden as something most grievous? Therefore, since evils have not been defined for everyone, it is impossible to expect judgment from God.” Peter said, “You cannot establish this, for it is evident to everyone that having intercourse with mothers is abominable, even if the Persians, who are one part of the whole, do not perceive the lawlessness of their abominable practice because of an evil custom. In the same way, Britons copulate openly before everyone and are not ashamed; others eat human flesh and feel no revulsion, others eat dogs’ flesh, and still others do unspeakable things. Judgments therefore must not be made by a perception that custom has diverted from what accords with nature. For being murdered is evil even if not everyone says so, since no one wishes to suffer it himself; and no one delights in theft when it punishes him personally. If, then, any single one at all is acknowledged to belong among sins, it is necessarily right to expect also a third judgment concerning sins.” When Peter had said these things, Simon answered, “This, then, is how you think matters concerning the evil one stand? Tell me.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"Ἑαυτὸν χρὴ κολάζειν τότε τῇ ἐγκρατείᾳ","chosen":"One must then punish oneself through self-control","rationale":"κολάζειν retains the passage’s punitive imagery, while ἐγκράτεια denotes restraint or self-control."},{"source_quote":"ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς τὴν κατ’ αὐτῶν εἰληφὼς ἐξουσίαν","chosen":"since from the beginning he has received authority against them","rationale":"The perfect participle presents the evil one as already possessing authority directed against evil people."},{"source_quote":"ἀιδίῳ περιβαλεῖν κολάσει","chosen":"cast oneself into everlasting punishment","rationale":"περιβάλλω literally suggests throwing or enveloping; “cast oneself into” preserves that force without adding a doctrinal specification of the punishment."},{"source_quote":"νόμῳ διαφέρει καὶ ἔθει","chosen":"does it differ by law and custom","rationale":"Simon contrasts what exists by nature with distinctions established by convention, law, and customary practice."},{"source_quote":"Βρεττανοὶ ἐμφανῶς ἐπὶ πάντων κοινωνοῦσι","chosen":"Britons copulate openly before everyone","rationale":"In this sexual context κοινωνοῦσι most naturally denotes intercourse; it could more generally suggest sharing sexual partners or women in common."},{"source_quote":"αἰσθήσει ὑπὸ ἔθους τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν ἐκτραπείσῃ","chosen":"by a perception that custom has diverted from what accords with nature","rationale":"The participle describes moral perception as turned away from the natural standard by habituation."},{"source_quote":"τρίτην κρίσιν","chosen":"a third judgment","rationale":"The ordinal is preserved without identifying or harmonizing the author’s proposed sequence of judgments."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"δικαίως τὸν κακῶς προδιωρισμένον ὀρθῶς ἔχειν εἰπόντος","issue":"The genitive participle εἰπόντος has no explicit genitive subject, while its accusative-infinitive statement permits more than one attachment. The translation supplies a generic speaker and takes τὸν κακῶς προδιωρισμένον as the infinitive’s subject. Alternatively, κακῶς may mean “badly” rather than “for evil,” and ὀρθῶς ἔχειν may mean “that it is right.”","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"ἔθει ..̓̀. παρὰ Πέρσαις","issue":"The selected edition contains a confirmed three-dot printed lacuna, with diacritical marks over the damaged position, between ἔθει and παρὰ Πέρσαις. The translation retains the three dots and supplies no missing connective or example marker.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"χαλεπώτ[ατον ἀπη]γόρευται","issue":"The supplied selected-edition text marks the letters ατον ἀπη with square brackets. The translation follows the resulting readable form χαλεπώτατον ἀπηγόρευται but does not treat the bracketed letters as unmarked evidence.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"κἂν οὖν ἑνὸς οὐδήποτε ὁμολογουμένου εἶναι ἁμαρτήματα","issue":"The singular genitive participle and the plural predicate ἁμαρτήματα create a number and constructional tension. The translation takes ἑνός as one act acknowledged to belong to the category of sins. A possible conjecture would make the participle active and refer to any individual acknowledging the acts as sins.","proposed_reading":"κἂν οὖν ἑνὸς οὐδήποτε ὁμολογοῦντος εἶναι ἁμαρτήματα","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"19.20","text":"Peter said, “We remember how our Lord and teacher, in giving us a command, said, ‘Guard the mysteries for me and for the sons of my house.’ For this reason he also ‘explained privately to his own disciples’ the mysteries of the kingdom of the heavens. But to you, who wage war against us and aim at nothing except our .... (whether true or false), it would be impious to speak the secret things. Nevertheless, so that some of those present may not think that I am devising a pretext because I am unable to answer what you have said, I will speak, first asking you: if there were no suffering, what would the evil one still be?” Simon said, “Nothing.” Peter said, “Is the evil, then, suffering and dying?” Simon said, “So it appears.” Peter said, “The evil therefore does not always subsist, nor indeed can it subsist, for suffering and dying are among the things that happen, neither of which occurs while soundness is present. For what is suffering except for something to be out of harmony? And what is death except the separation of a soul from a body? Thus, when harmony exists, suffering is not possible. Dying does not belong at all among things that subsist, because death is nothing, as I said, except the separation of a soul from a body. When this happens, the body, being naturally insensible, dissolves, while the soul, being sentient, continues alive. It follows that when harmony exists there can be neither suffering nor death; nor, indeed, are there deadly plants, venomous reptiles, or anything else of this kind whose end is death. Therefore, when immortality prevails, all things that have come into being will reasonably be manifest. This will indeed happen in this way whenever, because of righteousness, the human being becomes immortal while the Messiah’s peaceful kingdom prevails—when his temperament too is well-tempered, so that not acute........ impulses; and further, his knowledge is unerring, so that none of the evils as good π.......; and he will be suffering, so that he may not be mortal.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὰ μυστήρια","chosen":"the mysteries","rationale":"The term denotes teachings or realities restricted to insiders; the translation retains the author’s mystery terminology rather than paraphrasing it as ordinary information."},{"source_quote":"τὰ ἀπόρρητα","chosen":"the secret things","rationale":"ἀπόρρητα emphasizes matters not to be spoken or disclosed, distinguishing it from the preceding μυστήρια."},{"source_quote":"τὸ πονηρὸν","chosen":"the evil","rationale":"The neuter substantival form shifts from the personalized masculine “evil one” in the preceding question to evil considered as a phenomenon."},{"source_quote":"ὑπάρχει","chosen":"subsist","rationale":"The argument concerns whether evil has independent or enduring existence; “subsist” preserves that ontological force."},{"source_quote":"παρούσης εὐσθενείας","chosen":"while soundness is present","rationale":"εὐσθένεια can mean strength, vigor, or sound health; “soundness” fits the ensuing contrast with bodily disharmony."},{"source_quote":"ἡ δὲ ψυχὴ αἰσθητὴ οὖσα","chosen":"while the soul, being sentient","rationale":"In contrast with the body’s ἀναίσθητον, αἰσθητή denotes the capacity for sensation rather than being perceptible to someone else."},{"source_quote":"τῆς τοῦ χριστοῦ εἰρηνικῆς ἐπικρατούσης βασιλείας","chosen":"while the Messiah’s peaceful kingdom prevails","rationale":"χριστός functions independently as a title here, while the genitive absolute describes the kingdom’s prevailing rule."},{"source_quote":"ἡ κρᾶσις εὔκρατός","chosen":"his temperament too is well-tempered","rationale":"The cognate wording is retained: the person’s constitutional mixture is described as properly balanced."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"τὰ ἡμέτερα .... (εἴτε ἀληθῆ ὄντα εἴτε ψευδῆ)","issue":"A confirmed four-dot printed lacuna follows τὰ ἡμέτερα and removes the noun or expression qualified as either true or false. The translation retains all four dots and supplies no object.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"ἵνα μὴ ὀξείας........ ὁρμάς","issue":"A confirmed eight-dot printed lacuna interrupts the clause between ὀξείας and ὁρμάς, apparently removing wording needed to complete its syntax. The English deliberately remains fragmentary and retains all eight dots.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"ἵνα μή τι τῶν κακῶν ὡς ἀγαθὸν π....... τε ἀλγῶν ἔσται","issue":"A confirmed seven-dot printed lacuna follows the surviving initial π and removes wording needed to connect the comparison “as good” with the following clause. The surviving τε ἀλγῶν ἔσται literally yields “and he will be suffering,” which is retained despite its tension with the argument for immortality. No negation or verbal completion has been invented.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]}]}
